summary: Vatican City has no border controls or visa system of its own. You simply walk in from Rome, so entry is governed entirely by Italy's Schengen rules: EU citizens move freely, around 60 nationalities visit visa-free for 90 days in any 180, and everyone else needs an Italian Schengen visa.

passportValidity.text: Entry is via Italy, so Schengen rules apply: non-EU passports must be valid for at least 3 months beyond departure from the Schengen Area and issued within the last 10 years. There are no separate Vatican document checks.

travelInsurance.text: Travelers who need a Schengen visa for Italy must hold travel medical insurance covering at least €30,000. Visa-exempt visitors are not required to show it; the Vatican itself checks nothing at its boundary.

onwardTicket.text: The Vatican performs no border checks. Any onward-travel questions are asked by Italian officers at your point of entry into the Schengen Area.

proofOfFunds.text: No checks at the Vatican boundary. Italy may ask non-EU visitors to show adequate means of support when they enter the Schengen Area.

declarations.name: EES — Entry/Exit System (via Italy)
declarations.submitWindow: At the Schengen border on first entry
declarations.text: Non-EU travelers are registered biometrically in the EU Entry/Exit System when they first cross a Schengen external border — for Vatican visitors that means on arrival in Italy or another Schengen state, not at the Vatican itself.

declarations.name: ETIAS — European Travel Information and Authorization System (via Italy)

fee.notes: Free for under-18s and over-70s. Valid 3 years or until passport expiry.

declarations.text: Visa-exempt travelers will need an ETIAS authorization to enter the Schengen Area, and therefore to reach Vatican City through Italy. It is being phased in; check the official EU site for the current status.

currencyLimits.text: The EU rule applies on the way in: cash of €10,000 or more must be declared when entering or leaving the EU. There are no customs controls at the Vatican boundary itself.

notes: There are no customs checks between Rome and Vatican City. The boundary is an open square.
Airport-style security screening applies to enter St Peter's Basilica and the Vatican Museums.

payments.text: The Vatican uses the euro and its museum, post office and shop registers all take cards; Italian ATMs are a short walk away. Vatican-minted euro coins are collectors' items rather than everyday change.

safety.text: Vatican City itself is extremely safe and heavily policed. The real risk is pickpocketing in the dense crowds of St Peter's Square, the museum lines and on Rome's buses and metro serving the area.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — Italy Travel Advisory

bestTimeToVisit.text: Spring and fall offer mild weather and slightly thinner crowds; expect the biggest crushes at Easter, Christmas and on Wednesday mornings during papal audiences.

idp.text: Vatican City is a party to the 1949 Geneva Convention on Road Traffic but not to the 1968 Vienna one, so the International Driving Permit it is bound to recognize is the 1949 Geneva version. A permit issued under the 1968 Vienna Convention carries no treaty obligation here.

source.name: UN Treaty Collection — Convention on Road Traffic (Geneva, 1949), status of parties
source.instrument: Convention on Road Traffic, Geneva, 19 September 1949 (UNTS vol. 125, p. 3)

driving.text: Vatican City is a party to the 1949 Geneva Convention on Road Traffic but not to the 1968 Vienna one, so the International Driving Permit it is bound to recognize is the 1949 Geneva version. A permit issued under the 1968 Vienna Convention carries no treaty obligation here. Whether a permit is required in addition to a national license, and for how long a foreign license may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Vatican City yet.

source.name: UN Treaty Collection — Convention on Road Traffic (Geneva, 1949), status of parties

tips.text: There is no passport control between Rome and the Vatican — you cross an invisible line on St Peter's Square. Carry ID anyway, and expect airport-style security to enter the basilica and museums.
The dress code is enforced: shoulders and knees must be covered to enter St Peter's Basilica, the Vatican Museums and the Sistine Chapel — visitors in shorts or sleeveless tops are turned away.
Book Vatican Museums tickets on the official site (museivaticani.va) well in advance. The walk-up line can run to hours, and third-party resellers charge steep markups.
The Pope's general audience is held most Wednesday mornings in St Peter's Square — tickets are free but must be requested in advance through the Prefecture of the Papal Household.
Send a postcard from the Vatican post office. The state has its own stamps and postal system, a small tradition of a visit.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Vatican City?
faq.answer: There is no Vatican visa. Entry is through Italy, so Italian Schengen rules decide who gets in: EU and EFTA citizens enter freely, around 60 nationalities are visa-free for 90 days in any 180-day period, and everyone else needs a Schengen visa issued for Italy.

faq.question: Do I get a passport stamp for Vatican City?
faq.answer: No. There is no border control and no entry stamp — your Schengen stamps (or EES record) come from Italy. The souvenir alternative is a Vatican post office postmark on a postcard.

faq.question: Can tourists stay overnight in Vatican City?
faq.answer: No. There are no tourist hotels inside the walls; accommodation inside is reserved for clergy and official guests. Visitors stay in Rome, where the Borgo and Prati districts put you a few minutes' walk from St Peter's Square.

faq.question: How long can I stay in Vatican City?
faq.answer: Your allowance is whatever your Schengen status in Italy gives you — for visa-exempt visitors, 90 days in any 180-day period counted across the whole Schengen Area. In practice the Vatican is a day visit: the basilica, museums and gardens are all doable from Rome.

faq.question: Will I need ETIAS to visit the Vatican?
faq.answer: Effectively yes, once it becomes mandatory — not for the Vatican itself, which has no border checks, but to enter the Schengen Area through Italy on a visa-exempt passport. The €20 authorization is bought online at the official EU site only.
